data.why: A flatbed truck stands on the driveway in front of the garage, seen from the side with its chassis open, so the wheels, the rear steering motor, the tie rod and the spring all show. With front steering only, the tail swings out and knocks over a post. Rear steering turns the truck tightly, then in-phase at speed, then adds a failsafe spring. The camera starts on the truck, moves to the tail and rear axle for the fixes, and ends on the truck crabbing into the garage.

story.title: How four-wheel steering turns a giant truck like a compact

ideas.idea: if only the front wheels of a long truck steer, it cannot turn tight
the long body cannot pivot, so its tail swings out wide toward a post
the swinging tail clips the post and knocks it flat, which in a tight street means a crunched bumper
you bolt a steering motor onto the rear axle so the back wheels can turn too
a truck whose rear wheels steer as well is four-wheel steering
at a crawl the motor turns the rear wheels against the front ones, so the truck pivots in a tight circle like a compact
a Mercedes S-Class turns its rear wheels up to 10 degrees, which shrinks its turning circle by about two meters
at highway speed, turning the rear wheels against the front makes the tail whip around
above about 37 mph the rear wheels turn the same way as the front, so the truck tracks straight
turning the same way is in-phase steering, and the tight low-speed turn is counter-phase
if the motor fails, the rod can snap and leave the rear wheels stuck, so the truck veers
a spring pulls the rear wheels back to center and locks them straight
four-wheel steering is not four-wheel drive, even though all four wheels seem to be doing something
it only swivels the wheels left and right, and Honda's 1987 Prelude already did it
add a ceiling light and let the truck crab sideways into the garage
the truck now parks like a compact car, calm and finished
